claim: MxB is a type one interferon induced restriction factor.
source: The type one interferon induced restriction factor Myxovirus resistance B (MxB) restricts HIV-1 nuclear entry
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of MxB.

claim: MxB restricts HIV-1 nuclear entry.
source: The type one interferon induced restriction factor Myxovirus resistance B (MxB) restricts HIV-1 nuclear entry evidenced by inhibition of 2-LTR but not linear forms of viral DNA.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing inhibition of 2-LTR circles.

claim: MxB inhibits 2-LTR circle formation but not linear forms of viral DNA.
source: The type one interferon induced restriction factor Myxovirus resistance B (MxB) restricts HIV-1 nuclear entry evidenced by inhibition of 2-LTR but not linear forms of viral DNA.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by qPCR data in Figure 1D showing reduced 2-LTR circles but not RT products.

claim: The HIV-1 capsid is the key determinant of MxB sensitivity.
source: The HIV-1 capsid is the key determinant of MxB sensitivity
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by experiments showing capsid mutants have altered MxB sensitivity.

claim: HIV-1 capsid mutant P90A is defective for cyclophilin A and Nup358 recruitment.
source: cofactor binding defective HIV-1 capsid mutants P90A (defective for cyclophilin A and Nup358 recruitment)
evidence: Stated in abstract with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 capsid mutant N74D is defective for CPSF6 recruitment.
source: N74D (defective for CPSF6 recruitment)
evidence: Stated in abstract with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 capsid mutants P90A and N74D have reduced dependency on nuclear transport associated cofactors.
source: cofactor binding defective HIV-1 capsid mutants P90A (defective for cyclophilin A and Nup358 recruitment) and N74D (defective for CPSF6 recruitment) have reduced dependency on nuclear transport associated cofactors
evidence: Stated in abstract with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 capsid mutants P90A and N74D have altered integration targeting preferences.
source: cofactor binding defective HIV-1 capsid mutants P90A (defective for cyclophilin A and Nup358 recruitment) and N74D (defective for CPSF6 recruitment) have reduced dependency on nuclear transport associated cofactors, altered integration targeting preferences
evidence: Stated in abstract with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 capsid mutants P90A and N74D are not restricted by MxB expression.
source: cofactor binding defective HIV-1 capsid mutants P90A (defective for cyclophilin A and Nup358 recruitment) and N74D (defective for CPSF6 recruitment) have reduced dependency on nuclear transport associated cofactors, altered integration targeting preferences and are not restricted by MxB expression.
evidence: Stated in abstract and confirmed by experimental data in Figures 2A and 3A.

claim: Depleting CPSF6 to change nuclear import pathway does not impact MxB sensitivity.
source: We show that depleting CPSF6 to change nuclear import pathway does not impact MxB sensitivity
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing MxB sensitivity is retained after CPSF6 depletion.

claim: Mutants that recapitulate the effect of Cyclophilin A binding on capsid conformation and dynamics strongly impact MxB sensitivity.
source: mutants that recapitulate the effect of Cyclophilin A binding on capsid conformation and dynamics strongly impact MxB sensitivity
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by data in Figure 3G-J showing A92E and G94D mutations restore MxB sensitivity.

claim: HIV-1 primary isolates have different MxB sensitivities due to cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) selected differences in Gag sequence.
source: We demonstrate that HIV-1 primary isolates have different MxB sensitivities due to cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) selected differences in Gag sequence but similar cofactor dependencies.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by data in Figure 1E-H showing variable MxB sensitivity among primary isolates.

claim: HIV-1 primary isolates have similar cofactor dependencies despite different MxB sensitivities.
source: We demonstrate that HIV-1 primary isolates have different MxB sensitivities due to cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) selected differences in Gag sequence but similar cofactor dependencies.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by data in Figure 1I-P showing conserved sensitivity to cofactor depletion.

claim: Cyclophilin binding provides conformational flexibility to HIV-1 capsid facilitating simultaneous evasion of capsid-targeting restriction factors including TRIM5 as well as MxB.
source: We propose that cyclophilin binding provides conformational flexibility to HIV-1 capsid facilitating simultaneous evasion of capsid-targeting restriction factors including TRIM5 as well as MxB.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: MxA and MxB are interferon-induced, high molecular weight GTPases in humans.
source: Mx proteins (MxA and MxB in humans [Aebi et al., 1989]) are interferon-induced, high molecular weight, GTPases
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: Mx proteins have globular N-terminal domains forming an enzymatic active site and C-terminal leucine zipper domains connected by a hinge-like bundle-signalling element (BSE).
source: Mx proteins (MxA and MxB in humans [Aebi et al., 1989]) are interferon-induced, high molecular weight, GTPases with globular N-terminal domains forming an enzymatic active site and C-terminal leucine zipper domains connected by a hinge-like bundle-signalling element (BSE) (Fribourgh et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxA has antiviral activity against influenza A virus.
source: MxA has well-characterised antiviral activity against influenza A virus (Pavlovic et al., 1990)
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxA has antiviral activity against bunyaviruses.
source: MxA has well-characterised antiviral activity against influenza A virus (Pavlovic et al., 1990), bunyaviruses (Kochs et al., 2002)
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxA has antiviral activity against rhabdoviruses.
source: MxA has well-characterised antiviral activity against influenza A virus (Pavlovic et al., 1990), bunyaviruses (Kochs et al., 2002) and rhabdoviruses (Pavlovic et al., 1990)
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxB inhibits HIV-1 infection.
source: whereas closely related MxB has been shown to inhibit HIV-1 infection (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013)
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxB inhibits hepatitis C virus.
source: whereas closely related MxB has been shown to inhibit HIV-1 infection (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013) and more recently hepatitis C virus (Yi et al., 2019)
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxB inhibits herpesviruses.
source: whereas closely related MxB has been shown to inhibit HIV-1 infection (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013) and more recently hepatitis C virus (Yi et al., 2019) and herpesviruses (Crameri et al., 2018; Schilling et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy of MxB has revealed higher order oligomers and large helical assemblies.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy of MxB has revealed higher order oligomers and large helical assembles (Alvarez et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxB dimerisation and oligomerisation is important for anti-HIV activity.
source: MxB dimerisation and oligomerisation appears to be important for anti-HIV activity, but larger helical assemblies are thought not to be required (Alvarez et al., 2017; Buffone et al., 2015; Fricke et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: Larger helical assemblies of MxB are thought not to be required for anti-HIV activity.
source: MxB dimerisation and oligomerisation appears to be important for anti-HIV activity, but larger helical assemblies are thought not to be required (Alvarez et al., 2017; Buffone et al., 2015; Fricke et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: Mx GTPase activity is highly conserved through evolution and is functional in human MxB.
source: Mx GTPase activity is highly conserved through evolution and is functional in human MxB (King et al., 2004)
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxB GTPase activity is dispensable for MxB anti-HIV-1 activity.
source: Mx GTPase activity is highly conserved through evolution and is functional in human MxB (King et al., 2004), but surprisingly, is dispensable for MxB anti-HIV-1 activity (Goujon et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxA does not restrict HIV-1.
source: MxA does not restrict HIV-1 but the transfer of the N-terminal nuclear envelope targeting amino acids (1-26) from MxB to MxA generates a chimeric protein with anti-HIV-1 activity equivalent to the wild-type MxB protein (Goujon et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: Transfer of the N-terminal nuclear envelope targeting amino acids (1-26) from MxB to MxA generates a chimeric protein with anti-HIV-1 activity equivalent to wild-type MxB.
source: MxA does not restrict HIV-1 but the transfer of the N-terminal nuclear envelope targeting amino acids (1-26) from MxB to MxA generates a chimeric protein with anti-HIV-1 activity equivalent to the wild-type MxB protein (Goujon et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxB anti-HIV-1 activity depends on its amino terminal region.
source: This observation illustrates the dependence of MxB anti-HIV-1 activity on its amino terminal region
evidence: Inferred from the MxA/MxB chimera experiment cited.

claim: Protein location at the nuclear membrane, conveyed by the MxB N terminus, is important for anti-viral activity.
source: This observation illustrates the dependence of MxB anti-HIV-1 activity on its amino terminal region and suggests that protein location at the nuclear membrane, conveyed by the MxB N terminus, is important for anti-viral activity.
evidence: Inferred from the MxA/MxB chimera experiment.

claim: MxB is thought to suppress HIV-1 nuclear transport because it inhibits HIV-1 2-LTR circle formation but not viral DNA synthesis.
source: MxB is thought to suppress HIV-1 nuclear transport because it inhibits HIV-1 2-LTR circle formation but not viral DNA synthesis.
evidence: Stated in introduction based on experimental observations.

claim: Several studies have identified HIV-1 CA mutations that desensitise HIV-1 to MxB restriction.
source: Several studies have identified HIV-1 CA mutations that desensitise HIV-1 to MxB restriction (Busnadiego et al., 2014; Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2016)
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: Biochemical CA-MxB binding studies have suggested that MxB escape mutations in the capsid do not prevent MxB interacting with CA in vitro.
source: but biochemical CA-MxB binding studies have suggested that MxB escape mutations in the capsid do not prevent MxB interacting with CA in vitro (Fribourgh et al., 2014; Fricke et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: MxB can interact with various components of the nuclear pore complex via its N-terminal domain.
source: Recently, it has been suggested that MxB can interact with various components of the nuclear pore complex via its N-terminal domain (Dicks et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: Both Nup214 and TNPO1 are required for MxB nuclear envelope localisation.
source: Both Nup214 and TNPO1 were shown to be required for MxB nuclear envelope localisation, and for MxB restriction of HIV-1, through interaction with the triple arginine motif within the N-terminal domain of MxB.
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: Both Nup214 and TNPO1 are required for MxB restriction of HIV-1.
source: Both Nup214 and TNPO1 were shown to be required for MxB nuclear envelope localisation, and for MxB restriction of HIV-1, through interaction with the triple arginine motif within the N-terminal domain of MxB.
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: Nup214 and TNPO1 interact with the triple arginine motif within the N-terminal domain of MxB.
source: Both Nup214 and TNPO1 were shown to be required for MxB nuclear envelope localisation, and for MxB restriction of HIV-1, through interaction with the triple arginine motif within the N-terminal domain of MxB.
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation support.

claim: The cellular cofactors used by HIV-1 to enter the nucleus do not constitute a determinant of MxB sensitivity.
source: We find that the cellular cofactors used by HIV-1 to enter the nucleus, that is the nuclear entry mechanism, do not constitute a determinant of MxB sensitivity.
evidence: Stated in introduction as a finding of this study, supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The interaction of CypA with the classical reference strain R9 is essential for MxB sensitivity.
source: We also show that the interaction of CypA with the classical reference strain R9 is essential for MxB sensitivity
evidence: Stated in introduction as a finding, supported by data in Figure 3C showing CypA depletion rescues R9 from MxB.

claim: CypA interaction is not required for MxB sensitivity of a series of R9 mutants or divergent wild type HIV-1 Gag sequences.
source: We also show that the interaction of CypA with the classical reference strain R9 is essential for MxB sensitivity but that this interaction is not required for MxB sensitivity of a series of R9 mutants or divergent wild type HIV-1 Gag sequences.
evidence: Stated in introduction as a finding, supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: MxB sensitivity is determined by CA surface dynamics governed by CypA recruitment and CA sequence.
source: We propose that MxB sensitivity is determined by CA surface dynamics governed by CypA recruitment and CA sequence.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Upon IFN stimulation, MxB expression is strongly induced.
source: The expression of MxB is tightly controlled by the type one interferon (IFN) - JAK-STAT axis (Von Wussow et al., 1990) and upon IFN stimulation, MxB expression is strongly induced (Figure 1B)
evidence: Stated in results with citation and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B.

claim: MxB proteins localize to diffuse cytoplasmic puncta and to a distinct ring in the region of the nuclear envelope upon IFN stimulation.
source: and upon IFN stimulation, MxB expression is strongly induced (Figure 1B) and MxB proteins localize to diffuse cytoplasmic puncta and to a distinct ring in the region of the nuclear envelope, while the nucleus interior is largely devoid of MxB (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A.

claim: The nucleus interior is largely devoid of MxB upon IFN stimulation.
source: and MxB proteins localize to diffuse cytoplasmic puncta and to a distinct ring in the region of the nuclear envelope, while the nucleus interior is largely devoid of MxB (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A.

claim: Constitutive MxB expression is toxic.
source: Since we found constitutive MxB expression to be toxic
evidence: Stated as an observation in the results section.

claim: Induction of MxB expression in HEK293 cells with dox for 48 hr prior to infection results in MxB levels similar to those seen after IFN-β induction.
source: Importantly, induction of MxB expression in HEK293 cells with dox for 48 hr prior to infection, resulted in MxB levels similar to those seen after IFN-β induction (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B.

claim: MxB expression reduced the titre of HIV-1 GFP R9 by approximately 10-fold.
source: As previously reported, MxB expression reduced the titre of HIV-1 GFP R9 by approximately 10-fold (Figure 1C; Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dox induced MxB antiviral activity against HIV-1 GFP R9 was consistent in HEK293, monocytic cell line THP-1 and T cell line A3.01.
source: Dox induced MxB antiviral activity against HIV-1 GFP R9 was consistent in HEK293, monocytic cell line THP-1 and T cell line A3.01 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: MxB expression in HEK293 cells did not affect HIV-1 GFP R9 reverse transcription.
source: MxB expression in HEK293 cells did not effect HIV-1 GFP R9 reverse transcription (Figure 1D)
evidence: Stated in results and supported by qPCR data in Figure 1D.

claim: MxB expression reduced 2-LTR circles and integrated proviral DNA of HIV-1 GFP R9.
source: MxB expression in HEK293 cells did not effect HIV-1 GFP R9 reverse transcription (Figure 1D), but reduced 2-LTR circles and integrated proviral DNA (Figure 1D) as previously described (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013) consistent with suppression of viral nuclear entry.
evidence: Stated in results with citation support and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HIV-1 GFP constructs bearing gag genes from HIV-1(M) primary isolates have different MxB sensitivities of between 10 fold and 2-fold inhibition.
source: To our surprise we discovered quite different MxB sensitivities of between 10 fold and 2-fold inhibition, on MxB induction (Figure 1F,H).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 1F and 1H.

claim: HIV-1 CA mutant N74D is insensitive to depletion of HIV-1 nuclear entry cofactors Nup358, TNPO3, CPSF6 and to some degree Nup153.
source: For example, MxB-insensitive CA mutant N74D (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013) is insensitive to depletion of HIV-1 nuclear entry cofactors Nup358, TNPO3, CPSF6 and to some degree Nup153 (Achuthan et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2010; Schaller et al., 2011; Sowd et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 bearing CA P90A has reduced sensitivity to depletion of Nup358, TNPO3 and CPSF6.
source: HIV-1 bearing CA P90A, which alters the otherwise completely conserved CypA binding site and reduces CA affinity for CypA (Yoo et al., 1997) and Nup358 (Schaller et al., 2011), is completely insensitive to MxB restriction and also has reduced sensitivity to depletion of Nup358, TNPO3 and CPSF6.
evidence: Stated in results with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 bearing CA P90A is completely insensitive to MxB restriction.
source: HIV-1 bearing CA P90A, which alters the otherwise completely conserved CypA binding site and reduces CA affinity for CypA (Yoo et al., 1997) and Nup358 (Schaller et al., 2011), is completely insensitive to MxB restriction
evidence: Stated in results with citation support and confirmed by data in Figure 3A.

claim: HIV-1 CA mutants P90A and N74D have retargeted proviral integration preferences.
source: Both of these mutants also have retargeted proviral integration preferences consistent with altered nuclear entry mechanisms (Achuthan et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2010; Schaller et al., 2011; Sowd et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support.

claim: Viruses bearing both MxB sensitive and insensitive HIV-1(M) Gags had similar cofactor dependence, evidenced by similar sensitivities to stable depletions of TNPO3 or Nup358 in HeLa cells.
source: However, viruses bearing both MxB sensitive, and insensitive, HIV-1(M) Gags had similar cofactor dependence, evidenced by similar sensitivities to stable depletions (Figure 1K) of TNPO3 or Nup358 in HeLa cells (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 1I, 1J, and 1K.

claim: HIV-1 GFP bearing each of the divergent Gags were sensitive to ∆CPSF6 expression.
source: Again, HIV-1 GFP bearing each of the divergent Gags were sensitive to ∆CPSF6 expression (Figure 1N) consistent with CPSF6 use as a cofactor (Figure 1L,M).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 1L, 1M, and 1N.

claim: The CypA binding site was conserved in all of the Gags tested.
source: The CypA binding site was conserved in all of the Gags tested
evidence: Stated in results based on sequence analysis.

claim: Each virus tested was sensitive to expression of a human TRIM5-CypA chimera suggesting all tested viruses are able to bind CypA.
source: The CypA binding site was conserved in all of the Gags tested and concordantly, each virus was sensitive to expression of a human TRIM5-CypA chimera (Figure 1O and P) suggesting all tested viruses are able to bind CypA.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 1O and 1P.

claim: HIV-1 GFP R9 bearing CA mutant N74D was insensitive to MxB.
source: As reported, HIV-1 GFP R9 bearing CA mutant N74D, which does not bind the cellular cofactor CPSF6, was insensitive to MxB (Figure 2A,B)
evidence: Stated in results with citation support and shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: MxB induction did not strongly suppress HIV-1 CA N74D infection, viral DNA synthesis, or 2LTR circle formation.
source: As reported, HIV-1 GFP R9 bearing CA mutant N74D, which does not bind the cellular cofactor CPSF6, was insensitive to MxB (Figure 2A,B) and MxB induction did not strongly suppress infection (Figure 2A), viral DNA synthesis, or 2LTR circle formation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: CPSF6 depletion reduces HIV-1 R9 sensitivity to depletion of nuclear entry associated cofactors without impacting infectivity.
source: This is informative because, like CA mutation N74D, CPSF6 depletion reduces HIV-1 R9 sensitivity to depletion of nuclear entry associated cofactors without impacting infectivity (Lee et al., 2010; Ocwieja et al., 2011; Schaller et al., 2011; Sowd et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support.

claim: When CPSF6 was effectively depleted with shRNA, HIV-1 remained sensitive to MxB.
source: However, when we effectively depleted CPSF6 with shRNA (Figure 2D), HIV-1 remained sensitive to MxB (Figure 2C).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: In the absence of CPSF6, the MxB block to infection was accompanied by a reduction in 2LTR circles, suggesting MxB mediated suppression of nuclear entry was retained.
source: In the absence of CPSF6, the MxB block to infection was accompanied by a reduction in 2LTR circles, as in wild type cells, suggesting MxB mediated suppression of nuclear entry was retained (Figure 2C).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: This is the first occasion in which the effects of CPSF6 depletion and CA N74D mutation on HIV-1 infection differ.
source: To our knowledge this is the first occasion in which the effects of CPSF6 depletion and CA N74D mutation on HIV-1 infection differ (Lee et al., 2010; Ocwieja et al., 2011; Schaller et al., 2011; Sowd et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support.

claim: CPSF6 was found in the nucleus by immunostaining 293 T cells and this was not altered by MxB expression.
source: Importantly, CPSF6 was found in the nucleus by immunostaining 293 T cells and this was not altered by MxB expression suggesting that MxB does not inhibit HIV-1 by regulating CPSF6 traffic into the nucleus (Figure 2E).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2E.

claim: MxB does not inhibit HIV-1 by regulating CPSF6 traffic into the nucleus.
source: Importantly, CPSF6 was found in the nucleus by immunostaining 293 T cells and this was not altered by MxB expression suggesting that MxB does not inhibit HIV-1 by regulating CPSF6 traffic into the nucleus (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescence data showing CPSF6 localization is unchanged by MxB.

claim: HIV-1 bearing CA N74D is insensitive to MxB as a direct result of the CA mutation and not due to loss of CPSF6 recruitment.
source: Together, these observations suggest that HIV-1 bearing CA N74D is insensitive to MxB as a direct result of the CA mutation and not due to loss of CPSF6 recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing differential effects of N74D mutation versus CPSF6 depletion.

claim: Effective transient TNPO3 depletion reduced wild type HIV-1 GFP R9 infection in HEK293 cells but did not rescue infection from MxB.
source: Effective transient TNPO3 depletion (Figure 2G) reduced wild type HIV-1 GFP R9 infection in HEK293 cells but did not rescue infection from MxB (Figure 2F).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: TNPO3 depletion did not affect the sensitivity of HIV-1 CA P90A to MxB.
source: TNPO3 depletion also did not affect the sensitivity of HIV-1 CA P90A to MxB, which was insensitive to TNPO3 depletion as described (Schaller et al., 2011; Figure 2F).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The MxB block to HIV-1 nuclear entry is direct and not due to MxB influencing TNPO3 nuclear transport.
source: MxB induction also did not relocalise TNPO3, suggesting that the MxB block to HIV-1 nuclear entry is direct and not due to MxB influencing TNPO3 nuclear transport.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that TNPO3 localization is unchanged by MxB.

claim: Transient Nup358 depletion did not significantly impact HIV-1 GFP infectivity in HEK293 cells.
source: Transient Nup358 depletion did not significantly impact HIV-1 GFP infectivity in HEK293 cells (Figure 2I), despite efficient protein depletion (Figure 2J).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: Wild type HIV-1 GFP was fully sensitive to MxB after Nup358 depletion.
source: Importantly, wild type HIV-1 GFP was fully sensitive to MxB after Nup358 depletion and HIV-1 P90A MxB insensitivity was also not affected (Figure 2I).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 2I.

claim: HIV-1 P90A MxB insensitivity was not affected by Nup358 depletion.
source: Importantly, wild type HIV-1 GFP was fully sensitive to MxB after Nup358 depletion and HIV-1 P90A MxB insensitivity was also not affected (Figure 2I).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 2I.

claim: MxB restriction of HIV-1 is independent of the cofactors used for nuclear entry.
source: Together, these observations suggest that MxB restriction of HIV-1 is independent of the cofactors used for nuclear entry, and therefore mutation of Gag appears to be impacting MxB sensitivity in a more direct way.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing cofactor depletion does not affect MxB sensitivity.

claim: Mutation of Gag appears to be impacting MxB sensitivity in a more direct way.
source: Together, these observations suggest that MxB restriction of HIV-1 is independent of the cofactors used for nuclear entry, and therefore mutation of Gag appears to be impacting MxB sensitivity in a more direct way.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: HIV-1 CA P90A is insensitive to MxB demonstrating no reduction in HIV-1 P90A infectivity, 2LTR or proviral DNA levels after induction of MxB expression.
source: We verified that HIV-1 CA P90A is insensitive to MxB demonstrating no reduction in HIV-1 P90A infectivity (Figure 3A), 2LTR or proviral DNA levels (Figure 3B) after induction of MxB expression.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: CypA depletion fully rescues wild type HIV-1 GFP from MxB restriction, leading to a recovery of 2LTR circles and infectivity.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed the observation (Liu et al., 2013) that CypA depletion, here using shRNA (Figure 3D), fully rescues wild type HIV-1 GFP from MxB restriction, leading to a recovery of 2LTR circles and infectivity (Figure 3C).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support and shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Addition of the CypA inhibitor, cyclosporine A (CsA), at the time of infection, rescued wild type HIV-1 infectivity from MxB restriction.
source: Addition of the CypA inhibitor, cyclosporine A (CsA), at the time of infection, also rescued wild type HIV-1 infectivity from MxB restriction (Figure 3E), consistent with CypA recruitment by CA being necessary for MxB sensitivity.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: CypA recruitment by CA is necessary for MxB sensitivity of HIV-1 R9.
source: Addition of the CypA inhibitor, cyclosporine A (CsA), at the time of infection, also rescued wild type HIV-1 infectivity from MxB restriction (Figure 3E), consistent with CypA recruitment by CA being necessary for MxB sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CsA rescue experiment.

claim: HIV-1 infectivity can be almost completely rescued from MxB restriction by the addition of CsA up to 8 hr post infection, with the efficacy of CsA diminishing 24 hr post infection.
source: We also found that HIV-1 infectivity can be almost completely rescued from MxB restriction, by the addition of CsA, up to 8 hr post infection, with the efficacy of CsA diminishing 24 hr post infection (Figure 3F).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: Inhibition by MxB is reversible.
source: This shows that inhibition by MxB is reversible and suggests that the interaction between HIV-1 and MxB is not destructive, at least not immediately (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the time-of-addition CsA experiment.

claim: The interaction between HIV-1 and MxB is not destructive, at least not immediately.
source: This shows that inhibition by MxB is reversible and suggests that the interaction between HIV-1 and MxB is not destructive, at least not immediately (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reversibility of MxB inhibition.

claim: HIV-1 CA P90A treated with CsA during infection of MxB expressing cells showed no rescue to infectivity, consistent with P90A being resistant to MxB due to failure to recruit CypA.
source: In a control experiment, HIV-1 CA P90A was treated with CsA during infection of MxB expressing cells and we observed no rescue to infectivity, consistent with P90A being resistant to MxB due to failure to recruit CypA (Figure 3F).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: The A92E mutation was identified by selection of HIV-1 replicating mutants during CypA inhibition with CsA.
source: The A92E mutation was identified by selection of HIV-1 replicating mutants during CypA inhibition with CsA (Aberham et al., 1996).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support.

claim: The A92E mutation appears to recapitulate the effect of CypA binding by reducing the dynamics of the CypA binding loop on the surface of the CA leading to core stabilisation.
source: This mutation appears to recapitulate the effect of CypA binding by reducing the dynamics of the CypA binding loop on the surface of the CA (Lu et al., 2015) leading to core stabilisation (Li et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 bearing CA A92E infects HEK293 cells efficiently in the absence of CypA recruitment.
source: Thus, HIV-1 bearing CA A92E infects HEK293 cells efficiently, in the absence of CypA recruitment
evidence: Stated in results based on cited literature.

claim: Adding A92E to HIV-1 CA P90A rescued sensitivity to MxB.
source: In fact, adding A92E to HIV-1 CA P90A rescued sensitivity to MxB. Thus, MxB induction with dox restricted HIV-1 CA P90A A92E but not HIV-1 bearing CA P90A alone (Figure 3G).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: The A92E CA mutation rescued MxB sensitivity in the absence of CypA protein, after shRNA-mediated CypA depletion, and after CypA inhibition with CsA.
source: Importantly, the A92E CA mutation also rescued MxB sensitivity in the absence of CypA protein, after shRNA-mediated CypA depletion, and after CypA inhibition with CsA (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: HIV-1 sensitivity to MxB in the presence of CsA was also rescued by a second CsA escape mutant G94D.
source: HIV-1 sensitivity to MxB in the presence of CsA was also rescued by a second CsA escape mutant G94D (Figure 3J), which is also thought to recapitulate the effect of CypA binding by stabilising the CypA binding loop.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 3J.

claim: For HIV-1 R9, it is not CypA recruitment per se that is required for MxB sensitivity, but rather the conformational effect of CypA recruitment, likely the CypA mediated stabilisation of the CypA binding loop.
source: These data demonstrate that, for this particular HIV-1 isolate (HIV-1 R9), it is not CypA recruitment per se that is required for MxB sensitivity, but rather the conformational effect of CypA recruitment, likely the CypA mediated stabilisation of the CypA binding loop, which is recapitulated by the A92E and G94D mutations (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results with A92E and G94D mutations.

claim: HIV-1 GFP R9 was sensitive to MxB and CsA rescued infectivity but had itself a 2–3 fold inhibitory effect.
source: As reported, HIV-1 GFP R9 was sensitive to MxB and CsA rescued infectivity but had itself a 2–3 fold inhibitory effect.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 4A,B.

claim: HIV-1 GFP bearing clade H 90CF056 Gag was insensitive to MxB and CsA treatment.
source: HIV-1 GFP bearing clade H 90CF056 Gag was insensitive to MxB and CsA treatment.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Clade C 92BR025 Gag was insensitive to MxB but strongly inhibited by CsA treatment.
source: Clade C 92BR025 Gag was insensitive to MxB but strongly inhibited by CsA treatment.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Clade F 93BR020 Gag was MxB sensitive, but in a CsA insensitive way.
source: Clade F 93BR020 Gag was MxB sensitive, but in a CsA insensitive way.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Clade D 94UG114 Gag was weakly sensitive to MxB and CsA rescued infection from MxB but inhibited infection by 2–3 fold.
source: Clade D 94UG114 Gag was weakly sensitive to MxB and CsA rescued infection from MxB but inhibited infection by 2–3 fold (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: A threonine at position 210 correlated with MxB sensitivity and a serine correlated with MxB escape.
source: Indeed, a threonine at position 210 correlated with MxB sensitivity and a serine correlated with MxB escape (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Stated in results based on sequence analysis.

claim: There was no obvious association between the C-terminal CA sequence and sensitivity to CsA.
source: There was however, no obvious association between the C-terminal CA sequence and sensitivity to CsA.
evidence: Stated in results based on sequence analysis.

claim: The critical G89 and P90 residues required for CypA recruitment are conserved between HIV-1 R9 and 93BR020 Gags.
source: Inspection of the CypA binding loop sequence revealed that the critical G89 and P90 residues required for CypA recruitment are conserved but positions CA 86, 87, 92 and 96 are polymorphic between HIV-1 R9 and 93BR020 Gags (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Positions CA 86, 87, 92 and 96 are polymorphic between HIV-1 R9 and 93BR020 Gags.
source: Inspection of the CypA binding loop sequence revealed that the critical G89 and P90 residues required for CypA recruitment are conserved but positions CA 86, 87, 92 and 96 are polymorphic between HIV-1 R9 and 93BR020 Gags (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HIV-1 CA TQPI (V86T, H87Q, A92P M96I) lost both MxB and CsA sensitivity.
source: We found HIV-1 CA TQPI lost both MxB and CsA sensitivity and thus had a phenotype that was different to the parental R9 and 93BR020 Gags but similar to 90CF056 and 94UG114 Gags.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: Residue 96 is very close in space to another pair of polymorphic residues at positions 116 and 120 in the short alpha helix on the surface of the CA.
source: Further examination of HIV-1 CA structures indicated that residue 96 is very close in space to another pair of polymorphic residues at positions 116 and 120 in the short alpha helix on the surface of the CA (Figure 4E).
evidence: Stated in results and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: HIV-1 GFP CA TQPIQG (V86T, H87Q, A92P M96I, G116Q, H120G) behaved like the 93BR020 Gag bearing virus and was sensitive to MxB and this was not affected by CypA inhibition with CsA.
source: We found that this virus behaved like the 93BR020 Gag bearing virus and was sensitive to MxB and this was not affected by CypA inhibition with CsA.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: The double mutation HIV-1 R9 CA G116Q, H120G was not particularly different from the wild type HIV-1 R9 in either sensitivity to MxB or CsA.
source: Importantly, the double mutation HIV-1 R9 CA G116Q, H120G was not particularly different from the wild type HIV-1 R9 in either sensitivity to MxB or CsA indicating that the TQPI mutations are required to achieve the 93BR029 phenotype.
evidence: Stated in results and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: Five of six CA positions responsible for the different MxB and CsA sensitivity are highly variable.
source: Examination of CA sequence variation in a large (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or smaller (Figure 5) selection of HIV-1(M) sequences using Chromaclade (Monit et al., 2019) illustrated that five of six CA positions responsible for the different MxB and CsA sensitivity in Figure 4 are highly variable
evidence: Stated in results and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The residues required for CypA recruitment at positions 89 and 90 are completely conserved.
source: Examination of CA sequence variation in a large (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or smaller (Figure 5) selection of HIV-1(M) sequences using Chromaclade (Monit et al., 2019) illustrated that five of six CA positions responsible for the different MxB and CsA sensitivity in Figure 4 are highly variable, as opposed to the residues required for CypA recruitment at positions 89 and 90, which are completely conserved (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in results and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some CA positions, particularly 116 and 120, appear to have some degree of clade specificity.
source: Intriguingly, some positions, particularly 116 and 120 appear to have some degree of clade specificity.
evidence: Stated in results based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The regions around CA positions 116, 120 and 96 are particularly mobile relative to the rest of the protein.
source: Rendering CA crystal structures according to their atomic displacement parameters (B-factors) revealed that the regions around 116, 120 and 96 are particularly mobile relative to the rest of the protein (Figure 6).
evidence: Stated in results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: B-factors reflect the fluctuation of atoms about their average positions and provide important information about protein dynamics.
source: B-factors reflect the fluctuation of atoms about their average positions and provide important information about protein dynamics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B-factors in crystallography.

claim: The highly variable residues that influence MxB and CsA sensitivity are dynamic with 120, 116 and 96 close in space and likely influencing each other.
source: Thus these structures suggest that the highly variable residues that influence MxB and CsA sensitivity are dynamic with 120, 116 and 96 close in space and likely influencing each other.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the B-factor analysis and structural data.

claim: NMR studies have suggested that CypA influences CA by changing surface dynamics.
source: NMR studies have suggested that CypA, which influences some cases of MxB sensitivity, also influences CA by changing surface dynamics (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in results with citation support.

claim: MxB sensitivity is principally influenced by CA surface conformation and dynamics.
source: This observation, and the relatively large B-factors in CA structures for specific polymorphic residues which dictate MxB sensitivity, support the notion that MxB sensitivity is principally influenced by CA surface conformation and dynamics (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the B-factor analysis, NMR data, and experimental results.

claim: Direct recruitment of wild type CA, and not CA N74D, by MxB is the simplest explanation for the differential MxB sensitivity.
source: Direct recruitment of wild type CA, and not CA N74D, by MxB is the simplest explanation for these data.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Recent work has suggested that MxB may bind at the tri-hexamer interface to a strongly negatively charged patch composed of E71, E75 and E213 which may interact with the 11RRR13 motif of MxB.
source: Concordantly, recent work (Smaga et al., 2019) has suggested that MxB may bind at the tri-hexamer interface to a strongly negatively charged patch composed of E71, E75 and E213 which may interact with the 11RRR13 motif of MxB.
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation support.

claim: CA N74 lies between two of the putative MxB binding residues E71 and E75.
source: CA N74 lies between two of the putative MxB binding residues E71 and E75, but critically the N74 side chain extends away from the E71 and E75 side chains and into the CPSF6 binding pocket.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on structural analysis.

claim: The N74 side chain extends away from the E71 and E75 side chains and into the CPSF6 binding pocket.
source: CA N74 lies between two of the putative MxB binding residues E71 and E75, but critically the N74 side chain extends away from the E71 and E75 side chains and into the CPSF6 binding pocket.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on structural analysis.

claim: Mutation N74D replaces the amide side chain with a negatively charged acidic side chain in close spatial proximity to the positively charged K70.
source: Mutation N74D replaces the amide side chain with a negatively charged acidic side chain in close spatial proximity to the positively charged K70 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in discussion and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: N74D conformationally alters the capsid region to prevent both CPSF6 and MxB binding.
source: We therefore hypothesise that N74D conformationally alters this region of the capsid to prevent both CPSF6 and MxB binding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and experimental results.

claim: MxB recruitment to CA is required for restriction.
source: We assume that MxB recruitment to CA is required for restriction but it appears that the capacity to recruit CA in biochemical assays does not correlate with sensitivity to MxB restriction (Smaga et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption in the discussion.

claim: The capacity to recruit CA in biochemical assays does not correlate with sensitivity to MxB restriction.
source: We assume that MxB recruitment to CA is required for restriction but it appears that the capacity to recruit CA in biochemical assays does not correlate with sensitivity to MxB restriction (Smaga et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation support.

claim: CA mutation can influence the inhibitory effect of MxB binding, as well as influencing whether MxB binds at all.
source: We concur with these authors, hypothesising that CA mutation can influence the inhibitory effect of MxB binding, as well as influencing whether MxB binds at all.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: Despite insensitivity to MxB mediated inhibition of infectivity, proviral DNA levels of HIV-1 bearing CA P90A were increased by MxB induction.
source: Indeed, we observe that, despite insensitivity to MxB mediated inhibition of infectivity, proviral DNA levels of HIV-1 bearing CA P90A were increased by MxB induction (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in discussion and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: MxB still influences HIV-1 CA P90A, possibly at the level of nuclear entry and integration, despite not reducing the number of GFP positive cells.
source: This suggests that MxB still influences HIV-1 CA P90A, possibly at the level of nuclear entry and integration, despite not reducing the number of GFP positive cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of increased proviral DNA.

claim: MxB binds either directly or indirectly to incoming HIV-1 CA, at the nuclear rim where long MxB resides, and restriction occurs if CA is in an MxB sensitive conformation or state.
source: Thus our model, based on the literature and data herein, is that MxB binds either directly or indirectly to incoming HIV-1 CA, at the nuclear rim where long MxB resides, and restriction occurs if CA is in an MxB sensitive conformation or state.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and literature.

claim: CypA recruitment influences sensitivity to MxB restriction in a CA sequence sensitive way by influencing CA conformation.
source: Further, we conclude that CypA recruitment influences sensitivity to MxB restriction in a CA sequence sensitive way by influencing CA conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The effect of MxB restriction is to reduce nuclear entry of viral particles.
source: The effect of MxB restriction is to reduce nuclear entry of viral particles.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing reduced 2-LTR circles.

claim: CypA protects HIV-1 from restriction by TRIM5.
source: A recent study, demonstrating how CypA protects HIV-1 from restriction by TRIM5, likely explains inhibition of HIV-1 GFP infection by CsA in Figure 5 (Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation support.

claim: CypA does not protect infection from MxB but rather in some cases (R9, 94UG114) CypA causes MxB sensitivity.
source: It is striking that CypA does not protect infection from MxB but rather in some cases (R9, 94UG114) CypA causes MxB sensitivity.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental results.

claim: MxB provides less selective pressure on CA than TRIM5 because MxB expression is strictly controlled by IFN, while TRIM5 expression is enhanced by IFN but typically expressed at restrictive levels in unstimulated cells.
source: Thus perhaps MxB provides less selective pressure on CA than TRIM5 because MxB expression is strictly controlled by IFN, while TRIM5 expression is enhanced by IFN but typically expressed at restrictive levels in unstimulated cells (Jimenez-Guardeño et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 has adapted to avoid triggering IFN production.
source: We have proposed that HIV-1 has adapted to avoid triggering IFN production (Khan et al., 2020; Rasaiyaah et al., 2013; Sumner et al., 2019; Sumner et al., 2017) and this may reduce exposure to MxB.
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 adaptation to avoid triggering IFN production may reduce exposure to MxB.
source: We have proposed that HIV-1 has adapted to avoid triggering IFN production (Khan et al., 2020; Rasaiyaah et al., 2013; Sumner et al., 2019; Sumner et al., 2017) and this may reduce exposure to MxB.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: All the wild type Gag sequences tested were dependent on Nup358 and TNPO3 for maximal infectivity.
source: It is striking that cofactor use is not entirely flexible. All the wild type Gag sequences tested here were dependent on Nup358 and TNPO3 for maximal infectivity
evidence: Stated in discussion based on experimental results in Figure 1.

claim: All the wild type Gag sequences tested were sensitive to overexpression of mutant CPSF6 and TRIMCyp.
source: All the wild type Gag sequences tested here were dependent on Nup358 and TNPO3 for maximal infectivity and were sensitive to overexpression of mutant CPSF6 and TRIMCyp (Figure 1; Ikeda et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated in discussion based on experimental results in Figure 1.

claim: The difference between absolute dependence (Nup358, CPSF6, TNPO3) versus flexible (CypA) cofactor use likely reflects their role in the infectious cycle.
source: The difference between absolute dependence (Nup358, CPSF6, TNPO3) versus flexible (CypA) cofactor use likely reflects their role in the infectious cycle.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the discussion.

claim: Gag is under strong selective pressure from immune responses, particularly cytotoxic T lymphocytes presenting Gag derived peptides.
source: Gag is under strong selective pressure from immune responses, particularly cytotoxic T lymphocytes presenting Gag derived peptides (Carlson et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 must adapt to a selection of CTL escape mutations in CA and this is known to influence the relationship with specific co-factors e.g. CypA and CPSF6.
source: Thus HIV-1 must adapt to a selection of CTL escape mutations in CA and this is known to influence the relationship with specific co-factors e.g. CypA (Brockman et al., 2007; Leslie et al., 2004) and CPSF6 (Henning et al., 2014)
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation support.

claim: CTL escape mutations in CA influence sensitivity to restriction factors e.g. MxB and TRIM5α.
source: Thus HIV-1 must adapt to a selection of CTL escape mutations in CA and this is known to influence the relationship with specific co-factors e.g. CypA (Brockman et al., 2007; Leslie et al., 2004) and CPSF6 (Henning et al., 2014), and sensitivity to restriction factors e.g. MxB (Liu et al., 2015; Merindol et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2016) and TRIM5α (Battivelli et al., 2011; Granier et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation support.

claim: All HIV-1 sequences have been influenced by CTL exposure because CTL escape variants can be transmitted.
source: All HIV-1 sequences have been influenced by CTL exposure because CTL escape variants can be transmitted (Leslie et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 flexibly uses CypA and changing CA sequence to influence surface dynamics and conformation to achieve maximally infectious CA behaviour.
source: We interpret our data as suggesting a model in which HIV-1 flexibly uses CypA and changing CA sequence to influence surface dynamics and conformation to achieve maximally infectious CA behaviour.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: CypA recruitment facilitates CA sequence change and escape from immune pressure, by providing additional conformational options to retaining insensitivity to CA targeting restriction factors while retaining appropriate interactions with essential cofactors.
source: We hypothesise that CypA recruitment facilitates CA sequence change and escape from immune pressure, by providing additional conformational options to retaining insensitivity to CA targeting restriction factors while retaining appropriate interactions with essential cofactors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.
